content.title: Who is D. John Sauer? What to know about the lawyer leading the birthright citizenship case
content.text: Conflicting reports over Israeli strikes in Lebanon and threats from Iran spark market jitters, even as the White House insists the Strait of Hormuz remains open. WASHINGTON — A fragile ceasefire between the United States, Israel and Iran is already being tested, as conflicting claims over military activity and a key global shipping route raise new concerns about stability in the region. Iranian state media reported that the Strait of Hormuz has been closed again following Israeli strikes in Lebanon. The White House disputed those claims, calling them false, and said it expects the vital waterway to remain open without restrictions. The situation has been further complicated by renewed violence involving Hezbollah. The militant group has fired rockets into Israel, prompting Israeli strikes in Lebanon. U.S. officials say those actions do not violate the ceasefire, maintaining that Lebanon was never included in the agreement. Vice President J.D. Vance said the tensions stem from a “misunderstanding” about the scope of the deal. “I think the Iranians thought that the ceasefire included Lebanon, and it just didn’t,” Vance said in an interview Wednesday. “What we said is that the ceasefire would be focused on Iran and America’s allies, both Israel and the Gulf Arab states.” Iran has pushed back, accusing both the United States and Israel of violating the agreement and warning it could withdraw from planned talks. That uncertainty is already rippling through global markets. Oil prices, which initially dropped after the ceasefire announcement, are rising again, while overseas stocks slipped in early trading. The White House said it wants the Strait of Hormuz reopened immediately and without limitations, though questions remain about whether Iran could attempt to impose tolls on vessels passing through the critical corridor. “For now, that’s not something we’ve definitively accepted,” White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said, referring to the possibility of tolls. “The president was very clear … he wants to see the strait reopened immediately without limitation.” Despite the tensions, the ceasefire between the U.S. and Iran remains in place. Iran confirmed it will send a delegation to Pakistan for talks and possible negotiations with the United States, though it is unclear whether U.S. officials will participate. On Capitol Hill, Democrats led by Rep. Glenn Ivey of Maryland are expected to push for a War Powers resolution aimed at forcing a House vote on the president’s military authority. Republicans are expected to oppose the effort. Officials say the situation remains fluid, with developments unfolding rapidly.
